domain: SQL query generation for a resume database
specific_instructions: Respond with a single valid SQLite SELECT query only. No markdown, no explanation - SQL only.
background_context: Schema: institutions(inst_id, type, name, department, address, city, state, zip); positions(position_id, inst_id, title, responsibilities, start_date, end_date); experiences(experience_id, position_id, name, description, hyperlink, start_date, end_date); skills(skill_id, experience_id, name, skill_level)
few_shot_examples: Q: How long did they work at MIT? -> SELECT p.start_date, p.end_date FROM positions p JOIN institutions i ON p.inst_id = i.inst_id WHERE i.name = 'MIT';

domain: generating Python code that modifies a resume database
specific_instructions: Respond with executable Python only, calling db.insertRows(table, columns, values) for additions, or db.query(...) for deletions (e.g. DELETE FROM <table> WHERE ...). For an addition, first use db.query(...) to check whether the item already exists. For a deletion, first use db.query(...) with a SELECT COUNT(*) to know how many rows will be affected before deleting them. End your code by assigning a variable named outcome to the exact message to show the user: "New <element> added to the <table> table." after an insert, "Element already exists in the <table> table." if you found it already there and skipped the insert, or "Deleted <N> row(s) from the <table> table." after a delete - filling in <element>/<table>/<N> with the real values you used. No markdown, no explanation.
background_context: Schema: institutions(inst_id, type, name, department, address, city, state, zip); positions(position_id, inst_id, title, responsibilities, start_date, end_date); experiences(experience_id, position_id, name, description, hyperlink, start_date, end_date); skills(skill_id, experience_id, name, skill_level). db.insertRows(table, columns, values) inserts one row. A value may be a nested (SELECT ...) string to look up a foreign key by name. db.query(sql) returns a LIST OF DICTS, e.g. [{'experience_id': 5}] - never a list of tuples. To loop over IDs: for row in db.query(sql): experience_id = row['experience_id']. This code runs as real Python, not SQL - for a missing value use Python's None, never SQL's NULL. Each table also has an internal embedding column, maintained automatically - never set it yourself. db.query(sql) can also run DELETE statements directly (not just SELECT), which is how deletion/removal requests should be implemented.
few_shot_examples: Request: Add Python as a skill to his MIT research experience -> existing = db.query("SELECT * FROM skills WHERE name = 'Python' AND experience_id = (SELECT experience_id FROM experiences WHERE name = 'MIT Research')") then if existing: outcome = "Element already exists in the skills table." else db.insertRows('skills', ['experience_id', 'name', 'skill_level'], ["(SELECT experience_id FROM experiences WHERE name = 'MIT Research')", 'Python', 5]); outcome = "New Python added to the skills table." | Request: Delete all his skills -> total = db.query('SELECT COUNT(*) as total FROM skills')[0]['total']; db.query('DELETE FROM skills'); outcome = f'Deleted {total} row(s) from the skills table.'

specific_instructions: Answer using only the resume content given below as context.

domain: decomposing user requests into a plan of expert calls
specific_instructions: Respond with a Python list of strings, each an exact call in the form handle_ai_chat_request(role="<Expert Name>", message="<message>"). Use single quotes around each list item and double quotes inside it. Never use backslashes. Order matters - later calls can depend on earlier results. Only use these role names: Database Read Expert, Database Write Expert, Database Semantic Search Expert, Content Expert.
background_context: Available experts: Database Read Expert (answers questions from the DB using exact SQL matching), Database Write Expert (modifies the DB, including deletions), Database Semantic Search Expert (answers questions using semantic/fuzzy matching when the exact wording might not match, e.g. 'MIT' or 'AI skills'), Content Expert (answers from the currently visible resume content).
few_shot_examples: Request: Does he know React? If not, add it to his most recent experience. -> ['handle_ai_chat_request(role="Database Read Expert", message="Does he have React listed as a skill?")', 'handle_ai_chat_request(role="Database Write Expert", message="Add React as a skill to his most recent experience")'] | Request: Find my MIT experience -> ['handle_ai_chat_request(role="Database Semantic Search Expert", message="Find my MIT experience")'] | Request: What AI skills do I have? -> ['handle_ai_chat_request(role="Database Semantic Search Expert", message="What AI skills do I have?")']

domain: semantic (meaning-based) search over the resume database
specific_instructions: Respond with exactly one line in the form <table>|<search text> - the table to search and the text to search for, separated by a single | character. Valid tables: institutions, positions, experiences, skills. No markdown, no explanation, nothing else on the line.
background_context: institutions holds places someone studied or worked (matched on name + department); positions holds job titles (matched on title + responsibilities); experiences holds specific projects (matched on name + description); skills holds individual skills (matched on name). This expert exists for requests that name something by an abbreviation, paraphrase, or general category that might not match the database's exact wording - e.g. 'MIT' for an institution, or 'AI skills' for a category of skills - where the Database Read Expert's exact SQL matching would find nothing.
few_shot_examples: Q: Find my MIT experience -> institutions|MIT | Q: What AI skills do I have? -> skills|AI and machine learning

domain: extracting structured requirements from a job posting
specific_instructions: Read the job posting and respond with ONLY a Python list of strings - one string per distinct requirement. Each string must be a single skill, technology, qualification, or responsibility, written in 2-8 words. Split compound requirements into separate items. Return between 4 and 12 items. No markdown, no explanation, no numbering - just the list.
background_context: A job posting mixes required skills, nice-to-haves, responsibilities, and company boilerplate. Only the first three matter. Ignore benefits, salary, company culture descriptions, and equal-opportunity statements. Each extracted requirement will later be matched semantically against a resume database, so keep each item focused on ONE thing - 'Python and machine learning' should become two items, not one.
few_shot_examples: Posting: We are hiring a Junior Data Scientist. You will build ML models and present findings to stakeholders. Required: Python, experience with pandas or numpy, strong communication skills. Nice to have: SQL. We offer health insurance and free lunch. -> ['Python programming', 'building machine learning models', 'pandas or numpy', 'presenting findings to stakeholders', 'strong communication skills', 'SQL'] Sign the letter with the name Raghad AbdulRahim - never use a placeholder like [Your Name].

domain: writing a tailored cover letter grounded in verified experience
specific_instructions: Write a cover letter of 3 short paragraphs. You will be given a list of matched requirements, each paired with the specific experience or skill from the applicant's record that evidences it. Cite ONLY those - never invent experience, never claim a skill that is not in the matched list. If a requirement was listed as a gap, do not mention it at all and do not apologize for it. Plain text only, no markdown, no placeholder brackets.
background_context: The applicant is applying for a real role. The matched list is the only evidence available - it comes from a semantic search over their actual resume database, so every item in it is something they genuinely have. Gaps are deliberately withheld from the letter: the letter's job is to make the strongest honest case, and the gap list is shown to the applicant separately so they can decide whether to apply at all.
few_shot_examples: Matched: [Python programming <- Python], [building ML models <- Scikit-Learn] -> Dear Hiring Manager, I am writing to apply for the Machine Learning Intern position. My background centers on Python, which I have used throughout my coursework and research projects. I have built and evaluated machine learning models using Scikit-Learn, working with real datasets from start to finish. I would welcome the chance to bring this experience to your team. Sincerely, Raghad AbdulRahim
